notes: The canonical Uzbek expense frame: <merchant>+ablative -dan, then bare amount, no verb at all. Parser must strip -dan to find 'korzinka'. No currency word spoken so currency stays null.
'ketdi' (it went) is the most common expense verb and needs no object. Dative -ga on taksi.
'oldim' here means bought, not received — decided by the object 'non'. 6000 is written as digits >=1000 so it is literal, not 6 million.
'obed' is Russian-borrowed everyday Uzbek for lunch. Verbless.
'quydim' (I poured) is a fuel-only verb — a very strong category signal.
'kommunalka' is the umbrella word for the whole utility bill.
Amount comes before the verb; magnitude word 'million' spelled out.
'oylik' + 'tushdi' = the salary-landed frame. Unambiguous income.
Merchant with -dan plus an item noun that independently confirms the category.
Exact digit amount straight off the app receipt — no rounding, no magnitude word.
'tashladim' (I threw) is the idiom for topping up a phone balance. Dative -ga glued to a Latin brand name.
'dorixona' is a generic pharmacy, not a brand — merchant must stay null.
Minimal two-token utterance, dative marked.
Bare noun + amount, no suffix, no verb. The most compressed form there is.
'berdim' (I gave) marks cash handed over — expense, first person.
Uzum is a general marketplace, so the merchant gives NO category. Headphones fit no listed category — must fall back to 'other' rather than guessing household.
Private courses (English, IT) are a standard monthly line item in Tashkent.
'to'y' (wedding) money is a massive, culturally specific recurring expense. Maps to gifts; family is the plausible alternative.
'bozor' is a generic bazaar, not a named merchant.
'uchun' (for) is pure noise between the category noun and the amount.
'kecha' = yesterday. Contrast with 'kechqurun' = this evening — one syllable flips the date. 'chiqdi' = the bill came out to.

text: o'tgan juma kuni krosovka oldim 850 ming
notes: 'o'tgan' + weekday + 'kuni' -> last_<weekday>. The 'kuni' is noise once the weekday is captured.
Most Uzbek cars run on methane, so 'metan' is a fuel word, not a chemistry word. 'avvalgi kuni' = day before yesterday.

text: 3 kun oldin bolamga kiyim oldim 250 ming
notes: Two competing category signals: 'bolamga' (for my child -> family) and 'kiyim' (clothes -> clothing). The concrete item should win over the beneficiary.
TRAP: Click is a payment rail, not a merchant. 'orqali' (via) marks the payment channel — merchant must stay null. 'svet' = electricity.
Same rail trap as Click, but with the ablative -dan which normally introduces a merchant. Suffix shape alone cannot decide merchanthood.
Bare weekday with no o'tgan/shu is genuinely ambiguous in Uzbek. Past-tense 'berdim' pushes it to last_monday but confidence must drop.
QUANTITY TRAP: the 2 before '-ta' is a count. Only 78 ming is money. Also a multi-word brand with -dan glued to the second word.
Two numbers, only the second is a price. 'kg' is the disqualifier. A naive first-number-wins regex returns 2.
Classifier -ta marks the count. Note also that the price 6 ming is smaller than a normal grocery total — the parser must not 'fix' it.
Uzbek is verb-final but spoken word order is free. Category noun comes AFTER the verb here — position-based extraction fails.
MAGNITUDE ELLIPSIS, the central ambiguity of Uzbek money talk. Bare 45 in a taxi frame means 45 000 so'm. Nobody pays 45 so'm for anything. Currency still null.
Counter-case to the ellipsis rule: an explicit currency word blocks the x1000 scaling. 5 dollar is literally 5. No category signal at all -> other.
'ko'k' literally means green and is street slang for US dollars. Only a currency when adjacent to a number — 'ko'k ko'ylak' is a blue shirt. No verb, so even the expense/income direction is a guess.
Dative -ga glued to the AMOUNT, not to a place. Big purchases are habitually quoted in USD. 'telefon' here is a device, so communication would be wrong.
'yarim' is a multiplier of 0.5 applied to the following magnitude, with no digit anywhere in the string.
Here the dot IS a decimal point because a magnitude word follows. Compare '1.500' with no magnitude, which is a thousands separator. 'kontrakt' = university tuition.
'bir yarim' = one and a half, i.e. (1+0.5)x1000000. Contrast bare 'yarim million' = 0.5x. Position of the numeral before 'yarim' flips the arithmetic.
The -lik suffix means 'worth of'. Amount is still 20000, but the parser must not treat 'minglik' as an unknown token and drop the whole number.
Accusative -ni on the object and dative -ga on the amount. Both suffixes must be stripped before matching.
NO AMOUNT AT ALL. Valid utterance, valid category, amount null — the app must prompt. Parser must not hallucinate a number.
Same verb 'oldim' as 'non oldim' but the opposite direction. Only the object noun 'oylik' flips expense to income. This pair is the single most important disambiguation in Uzbek.
NEGATION. '-madim' is the negative past suffix. There is no transaction here at all; confidence must be low enough that the app refuses to log it.
FUTURE INTENT, not a transaction. 'to'lashim kerak' = I must pay. 'ertaga' has no slot in the date enum, so date stays null. Everything looks parseable, which is exactly the danger.
Borrowing increases cash but is not real income. Best available mapping is other_income with a note; confidence low so the user can correct.
Mirror of the previous case. 'akamga' would suggest family, but lending is not a family expense — money is expected back. Deliberately kept as 'other'.
'tushdi' guarantees income direction but says nothing about the source. Must NOT default to salary just because the amount looks like a salary.

expected.note: naqd yechish — cash withdrawal, not a real expense

notes: An ATM withdrawal moves money between the user's own pockets. It looks exactly like an expense ('kartadan' + amount) and must be suppressed.
3rd person plural '-ishdi' = they gave back. The plural suffix is what marks direction; 'qaytarib berdim' would be the opposite.

TWO TRANSACTIONS in one breath, joined by 'keyin' (then). Convention: expected = first transaction. Second = {expense, 20000, null, transport, null}. Parser must split on keyin/va/, and emit two records.

Two items with no connector at all — just alternating noun/amount pairs. Expected = first. Second = {expense, 12000, null, groceries, note 'sut'}. Could also legitimately be merged into one 18000 grocery run.
'marta' (times) is a frequency classifier, so 3 is not money. The 60 ming is the day's total, one record not three.
Regular cash support to parents is a normal monthly line. Possessive -m + dative -ga stacked on 'ona'.
'ovqat' alone means dining, but 'mushukka' (for the cat) overrides it to pets. Beneficiary beats item here — the opposite of the bolamga/kiyim case.
Religious almsgiving, a routine category for many users.
'ushlab qoldi' = they withheld it. Passive-ish framing with a 3rd person verb but still the user's expense.
Latin brand name inside an Uzbek utterance, no suffix attached.

COMPOUND AMOUNT with an elided second magnitude: '3 mln 200' = 3 200 000, because the trailing 200 inherits 'ming'. Naive parsing gives 3000000 or 200. Also 'dubayga' is a destination, not a merchant.
'gaz puli' = the household gas BILL -> utilities. Contrast the next line where the same word means car fuel. 'puli' (its money) is the disambiguator.
Same word 'gaz', opposite category, decided purely by the verb 'quydim' (poured into the tank). Deliberate minimal pair with the previous line.
TYPO: dropped vowel in the suffix ('korzinkadn'). Merchant matching must be fuzzy/edit-distance tolerant, not exact.
'taxi' spelled the English way with an Uzbek dative suffix — a very common hybrid on Latin keyboards.
'sum' is the apostrophe-less spelling of so'm and DOES set currency=UZS. Digits already literal, so no scaling.
Space inside the digit run is a thousands separator, not two numbers. Two items but ONE amount, so this is a single record — unlike the 'non 6 ming sut 12 ming' case.
Amount fully spelled as words with the dative -ga glued onto the CURRENCY word ('so'mga'). No digits anywhere.
Additive numeral: yigirma(20)+besh(5)=25, then x1000. No conjunction between the words — pure concatenation.
Number word + magnitude + currency, then a bare category noun with no suffix or verb.

text: ikki yuz o'ttiz ming ketdi bugun
notes: Three-word numeral: ikki(2) x yuz(100) + o'ttiz(30) = 230, then x1000. Multiplication and addition mixed in one span, with no category anywhere.
TRAP-ADJACENT: 'buyurtma' is listed as a freelance INCOME keyword, but here 'buyurtma qildim' means I placed an order. The -dim suffix and the merchant settle it as an expense.
Brand clipped to its first word ('Oqtepa' for Oqtepa Lavash), which is how everyone actually says it.
Amount lands in the middle, item list trails at the end with no connectors — classic dictation rhythm.
Magnitude ellipsis combined with a merchant. Two tokens total. 40 so'm is not a thing; 40 000 at a supermarket is normal.
'nasiya' = buy-now-pay-later, hugely popular in Uzbekistan. The full 8 mln was NOT paid today — the app may want to model instalments, so confidence is capped.
'foiz' (percent) marks 20 as a rate, not money. The real amount is the post-discount 160 ming.
THIRD-PARTY PAYER. Verb is 'to'ladi' (he paid), not 'to'ladim'. The user spent nothing. One missing -m inverts the whole record.
PRICE COMMENTARY, not a purchase. 'narxi' = its price and '-ibdi' is the reportative/hearsay past. Looks like a perfect fuel expense to a keyword matcher.
NOT A TRANSACTION AT ALL. Merchant present, locative suffix present, zero money. 'ishlayman' = I work. The parser must be able to output nothing.
'bordim' (I went) implies payment when the destination is a service provider.
Causative verb 'davolatdim' (I had it treated). Dentistry is a big-ticket health item.
Apostrophe dropped ('bogchaga' for bog'chaga). Kindergarten fees classed as education, though family is arguable.
Freelance earnings are almost always quoted in USD. Explicit currency blocks any scaling.
Mid-month salary advance is standard in Uzbekistan and maps to salary. Third instance of 'oldim' meaning received, not bought.
'k' as a thousands suffix, borrowed from chat English. Young Tashkent users type this constantly.
Bare weekday again -> last_<weekday> with reduced confidence. Note the doubled consonant in the dative 'akvaparkka'.
RECURRING RULE, not a dated event. 'har oy' (every month) has no date slot; the app should offer to create a subscription instead of one transaction.
'o'tgan hafta' (last week) has NO slot in the date enum, so date must be null and the phrase preserved in note. Also another elided-magnitude compound: 3 mln 800 = 3 800 000.
Magnitude ellipsis on a top-up. 20 000 so'm is a standard airtime top-up; 20 so'm is meaningless.

text: kir yuvish kukuni va salfetka 78 ming
notes: Two items joined by 'va' but ONE amount — must NOT be split, unlike the two-amount cases. The number of amounts, not items, decides.
Three-way pull: 'atir' (perfume -> beauty), 'xotinimga' (for my wife -> family), bought as a present -> gifts. Genuinely contested; any of the three is defensible.
'ishga' (to work) is a destination, not a category. Must not be mistaken for a work-related expense type.
TRAP: 'tushdi' is normally the strongest INCOME verb, but a traffic fine that 'landed' is money leaving. The noun beats the verb.
Approximative -cha ('about 10 dollars') glued onto the currency word. Amount is an estimate — confidence should reflect that.
SCRIPT SWITCH mid-utterance — the user changed keyboards after typing the brand. Tokenisation must be per-token, not per-utterance.
Reverse mix: Cyrillic brand, Latin magnitude word. Both scripts must normalise to the same internal key.
Three-way mix: Cyrillic date word, Latin brand with a Latin suffix, Cyrillic magnitude.
Latin category noun, Cyrillic verb and magnitude — autocorrect and keyboard switching produce this constantly.
Cyrillic income noun with possessive, Latin abbreviation and verb.
The canonical frame in Cyrillic. Brand must normalise to the Latin canonical form 'Korzinka'.
Cyrillic mirror of the basic taxi frame.
'олдим' as bought, decided by the object 'нон'.
'млн' is the Cyrillic million abbreviation.
Note ў — Cyrillic Uzbek uses ў/қ/ғ/ҳ, which plain Russian keyboards lack, so users often substitute у/к/г/х.
Cyrillic fuel frame with the specific letter қ.
'бозор' is generic, so merchant stays null despite the -дан suffix that usually flags a merchant.
Wedding envelope money, one of the largest irregular expenses in an Uzbek household budget.
Place noun carries the category with no item mentioned.
Home internet maps to communication rather than utilities.
Cyrillic spelling of the Beeline brand plus dative. Must map to the Latin canonical 'Beeline'.
DATE TRAP: 'кечқурун' = this evening (today), NOT 'кеча' = yesterday. The stems look nearly identical.
1st person PLURAL 'бордик' (we went) — still the user's own expense.
Item list with no separators, amount last.
Havas written with х rather than ҳ — the substitution ordinary Russian keyboards force.
Merchant alone supplies the category.
No suffix on the brand at all — bare juxtaposition.
Multi-word brand where the ablative attaches to the SECOND word, so the merchant span is discontinuous with the suffix.
Elided-magnitude compound in Cyrillic: 3 млн 500 = 3 500 000, with the trailing 500 inheriting 'минг'.
University tuition is paid in large lump sums — the parser must not treat 12 mln as an outlier to be rejected.
Verbless dative frame.
Cyrillic mirror of the dentistry case.
Generic clothing purchase.
Locative -да on a long compound noun (сартарош+хона+да).
'овқат' would mean dining on its own; 'мушукка' redirects it to pets.
Note the letter қ, absent from Russian keyboards; users often type садака.
A Latin brand transliterated into Cyrillic — brand matching must run after script normalisation.
Native compound (авиа+чипта) rather than the Russian-borrowed 'авиабилет'.
'бир кеча' means ONE NIGHT here, not 'one yesterday'. Same word 'кеча' that elsewhere means yesterday — the preceding numeral kills the date reading.
Plural -лар + dative -га stacked. Pocket money for the kids.
Another elided-magnitude compound. Carpets are a standard large household purchase.
Russian-borrowed beauty vocabulary written in Cyrillic.
Traffic fine. Unlike the 'жарима тушди' variant, here the verb already agrees with the expense direction.
Explicit USD blocks scaling; 500 stays 500.
'олдим' as received. The noun is the only signal.
Compound amount with BOTH magnitudes spelled out — easier than the elided form but still needs summation, not concatenation.
Small-trade profit. 'фойда' is the business-income keyword; the ablative -дан marks the source, not a merchant.
'фоиз' means both percent and interest. Here it is interest income; in '20 фоиз чегирма' it is a rate.
DIRECTION TRAP: 'берди' (he gave) = income, 'бердим' (I gave) = expense. A single -м separates them and the family noun is present in both.
'қайтди' (came back) is the refund verb.
Two-token magnitude ellipsis in Cyrillic. The shortest realistic real-world input.
Literal 5 with explicit currency and no category or verb — direction itself is a coin flip, hence very low confidence.
Cyrillic form of the 'green' dollar slang. 'бердим' fixes the direction as expense.
Quantity spelled as a WORD ('икки кило'), so a digit-only quantity filter misses it entirely.
'дона' is a classifier just like '-та'. The word-number 'уч' before it is a count.
Explicit 'ўтган' removes the weekday ambiguity, so confidence can stay high.
Cyrillic 'аввалги куни'. Must NOT be confused with 'ўтган куни', which is the vague 'the other day'.
DATE TRAP: 'ўтган куни' looks like 'аввалги куни' but means the vague 'the other day'. It must yield date=null, not day_before_yesterday.
Cyrillic negation with '-мадим'. Contains the buy-verb stem 'ол-' and the date word, so keyword matchers happily log a phantom expense.
Lending out: cash leaves but net worth is unchanged. Not a real expense category.
Income direction is certain, source is not. Must resist defaulting to salary on amount size alone.
Cyrillic 'клик' is still the payment rail Click and still must not become the merchant.
Two amounts, one trailing verb covering both. Expected = first; second = {expense, 14000, null, groceries, note 'сут'}.
Methane fill-ups are cheap, so 45 000 so'm is a realistic full tank — the ellipsis reading is the only sensible one.
Cyrillic transliteration of the Uzmobile brand with the dative glued on.
Russian loanword in Cyrillic with Uzbek case marking.
Word numeral 'ўн беш' = 15. The dative sits on the category noun, which trails the amount.
Amount and NOTHING else. No verb, no category, no currency. Direction must be assumed (expense is the safe default) with low confidence.
Both magnitudes explicit, so summation is unambiguous. Compare the elided '3 млн 800'.
Two transactions in the SAME category joined by 'ва'. Expected = first; second = {expense, 300000, null, gifts, note 'совға'}. Same-category pairs are the easiest to wrongly merge.
NEGATED INCOME: the salary has NOT arrived. Contains 'маош' and the stem 'туш-', the two strongest salary signals, so a naive parser logs a salary that never happened.

text: икки кун олдин Uzumdan 2 та футболка 180 минг
notes: Everything at once: word-number date offset ('икки кун олдин'), Latin brand in a Cyrillic sentence, a -та quantity, and the real amount last.
'бир ҳафта бурун' (a week ago) has no date slot — 7_days_ago would be an over-precise invention, so date must be null with the phrase kept in note.
'юз минг' = 100 x 1000 spelled as words, plus an explicit сўм. Causative-passive verb 'ёздиришди' (they wrote me up) still means the user pays.

text: kecha oqshom 3 kishi bo'lib restoranda 420 ming
notes: '3 kishi' (3 people) is yet another quantity shape with no classifier suffix. 'kecha oqshom' = yesterday evening, so the date is yesterday, not today.
'yigirmata' fuses the number word and the classifier into one token, so 20 is a count. 'ma'raka' (memorial gathering) is a culturally specific obligation expense — gifts or family, both defensible.

text: kartamdan avtomat 89 ming yechildi obuna uchun
notes: PASSIVE voice ('yechildi' = it was deducted) with no first-person agent anywhere. Contrast the active 'yechdim' withdrawal, which is NOT an expense — same stem, opposite treatment.
'Чорсу' is a named bazaar, so unlike the generic 'бозор' it IS a merchant. The two look identical syntactically.
Adjectival 'кечаги' (yesterday's) rather than the adverb 'кеча'. Trailing copula 'эди' is noise.
Tashkent rents are quoted in USD almost universally even though payment happens in so'm. 300 is literal, never 300 000.
MAGNITUDE ON A FOREIGN CURRENCY: 'минг доллар' = 40 000 USD, so the x1000 multiplier applies to USD, not so'm. Also a property sale, which is income but not any listed source.
District hot-water billing is separate from cold water and from gas in Uzbek apartment blocks.
Accusative -ни on the animal, dative -га on the service. Compound verb 'олиб бордим' (took along) is not a purchase verb but the expense is real.
Contains a stray Latin 'a' inside 'неваpамга' from a keyboard slip — a real mixed-script typo at the CHARACTER level, not the word level. 'совға' pushes gifts over family.
Religious donation. Note ҳ, another letter missing from Russian keyboards (often typed as х).
Flowers default to gifts, though they could be household decoration — genuinely underdetermined by two tokens.
'литр' is a unit, so the word-number 'ўн' before it is a volume, not money. Third distinct quantity shape after -та/кг and дона.

text: шанба куни тўйга бордик 1 млн бердим
notes: Bare weekday (ambiguous), TWO verbs ('бордик' we went, 'бердим' I gave) but only one amount, so one record — the verb count does not predict the transaction count.
Elided-magnitude compound (8 500 000) plus a 3rd-person-plural verb 'ўтказишди' (they transferred) that still means income to the user.
Labour-migrant remittance from Russia — a huge real flow. 'минг' multiplies a NON-so'm currency again, and 'юборди' (he sent) is 3rd person, hence income.
Kazakh tenge from a border/shopping trip. A foreign city name in the locative should route to travel, and 'тенге' must not be confused with the Uzbek so'm.
Card cashback. Small income amounts are common and must not be filtered out as noise.
TRAP: 'телефонга' looks like a phone top-up (communication) but this is a screen repair. There is no electronics/repair category, so 'other' is the honest answer.
Magnitude ellipsis on a service. A haircut costs 40 000 so'm, never 40 so'm.
Genitive -нинг + dative -га chained across two words. 'болам' pulls toward family but 'контракт' (tuition) wins.
A DAILY TOTAL, not one purchase. 'ҳамма нарсага' (on everything) explicitly refuses a category — the app should log it as an uncategorised lump.

text: дўконда қарзим бор эди уздим 180 минг
notes: Paying off a running tab at the corner shop — the classic 'дафтарга ёзиб қўйиш' credit. Cash leaves today for groceries bought earlier, so the date is genuinely contested.
IMPORTANT COUNTER-CASE to the ellipsis rule: 2 минг really is 2 000 so'm, the actual bus fare. Small amounts are legitimate and must not be inflated to 2 000 000.
Word-number date offset ('уч кун олдин') that must still resolve to the numeric 3_days_ago slot. USD subscriptions are normal.
'битта' fuses бир+та into one token, so the count is hidden inside a single word. 'бўпти' is the contracted colloquial form of 'бўлибди'.
